quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Opinion: The Case for a Shorter Week] Last year, our council tested a four-day working week for its office staff, with no reduction in pay. The results were striking: sick days fell by a quarter, and the number of resident complaints answered within 48 hours rose from 71 percent to 86 percent. Critics argue that other employers could not afford the same experiment, but that misses the point. Productivity does not rise because people work fewer hours; it rises because they stop wasting the hours they have. Any manager who has sat through a pointless Friday afternoon meeting knows this to be true. It is time other employers followed the council's lead.
quests.question: Which of the following is presented as a fact rather than an opinion?
options: Productivity rises because people stop wasting hours.
Sick days fell by a quarter during the trial.
Other employers should follow the council.
Friday afternoon meetings are pointless.
quests.correctAnswer: Sick days fell by a quarter during the trial.
quests.hint: A fact can be checked with figures or records; an opinion is a judgment.
quests.explanation: The drop in sick days is a reported result of the trial. The other statements are the writer's views or recommendations.
quests.evidenceLine: sick days fell by a quarter

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Letter from Customer Relations] Dear Mr. Fraser, thank you for your letter of 9 May regarding flight BX204. We are sorry that your flight was cancelled at short notice and that you spent six hours at the airport trying to find another one. Under the airline's policy, passengers whose flights are cancelled less than 14 days before departure are entitled to a refund or a seat on the next available flight; compensation is paid only when the cancellation is caused by something within the airline's control. Our records show that your flight was cancelled because a storm closed the airport, which we classify as outside our control. We have therefore refunded your ticket in full but are unable to offer further compensation. We hope to welcome you on board again.
quests.question: Why was Mr. Fraser not offered compensation?
options: He did not complain within the time limit.
He had already accepted a seat on another flight.
He waited fewer than six hours at the airport.
The storm was outside the airline's control.
quests.correctAnswer: The storm was outside the airline's control.
quests.hint: Compare the condition for paying compensation with the cause of the cancellation.
quests.explanation: Compensation is paid only when the airline could control the cause. A storm closing the airport is classed as outside its control.
quests.evidenceLine: outside our control

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [The Quiet Table] Ms. Haddad had eaten lunch at the same corner table for eleven years, and Joel, the waiter, knew her order without asking: a bowl of mushroom soup and black tea. Today she arrived at twelve, as always, but she sat with her coat on and left the menu closed. Joel brought the soup anyway. She thanked him, looked at it, and pushed it gently aside. "Everything all right?" he asked. She smiled in a way that did not reach her eyes. "My husband's birthday," she said. "He always ordered the fish." Joel nodded, took the soup away, and came back with a plate of grilled fish, which he set down without a word.
quests.question: What can be inferred about Ms. Haddad's husband?
options: He is no longer there to share the meal.
He is the chef who works in the kitchen.
He works nearby and visits her at lunch.
He dislikes the café and refuses to come.
quests.correctAnswer: He is no longer there to share the meal.
quests.hint: Notice the tense of the verb in her last sentence.
quests.explanation: She says he "always ordered" the fish and mentions his birthday, which suggests he is no longer with her.
quests.evidenceLine: He always ordered the fish

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Handwriting or Typing?] Many students assume that typing notes is better because it is faster. A study at one university tested this by asking two groups to take notes on the same lecture, one by hand and one on laptops. Typists wrote nearly twice as many words, but when both groups were quizzed a week later, the handwriting group scored higher on questions that required understanding ideas. The researchers suggest that because handwriting is slower, students must summarize as they go, which forces them to think about the material. They caution, however, that the study was small, and that students who type selectively might gain similar benefits.
quests.question: What did the typists do better than the handwriters?
options: They scored higher on questions about ideas.
They wrote more words.
They summarized the lecture more effectively.
They enjoyed the lecture more.
quests.correctAnswer: They wrote more words.
quests.hint: Separate what was measured during the lecture from what was measured later.
quests.explanation: The passage says typists wrote nearly twice as many words; the handwriting group did better on the later quiz.
quests.evidenceLine: Typists wrote nearly twice as many words

quests.passage: [Security Deposit Policy] Your security deposit, equal to one month's rent, is held in a protected account for the length of your tenancy. When you leave, we will inspect the property within five working days. Any deductions for damage beyond normal wear and tear will be itemized in writing, and the remaining deposit will be returned within ten working days of the inspection. Cleaning costs are deducted only if the property is left in a worse condition than shown in the entry photographs. If you disagree with a deduction, you have 14 days from receiving the itemized list to dispute it in writing; after that, the amount is final.

options: Within five working days of leaving
Within fourteen days of leaving
Within ten working days of the inspection
Within one month
quests.correctAnswer: Within ten working days of the inspection
quests.hint: The deadline is counted from the inspection, not from the day the tenant leaves.
quests.explanation: The policy says the remaining deposit is returned within ten working days of the inspection.
quests.evidenceLine: returned within ten working days of the inspection

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Book Review: The Salt Road] Nora Vance's account of traveling the old salt trade routes is easy to admire and, at times, frustrating to read. Her descriptions of the desert towns are vivid enough that I found myself checking my own water bottle, and the chapter on the caravan guides is a small masterpiece. Yet the book keeps promising an argument it never delivers. Vance hints repeatedly that the salt trade shaped the region's politics, then retreats into anecdote each time she approaches the point. Readers who enjoy atmosphere will be rewarded; those hoping for analysis will close the final page feeling short-changed.
quests.question: What is the reviewer's overall judgment of the book?
options: Entirely negative, finding nothing to admire in the writing at all
Mixed: admiring the description but disappointed by the lack of analysis
Entirely positive, finding nothing at all to criticize in the book
Neutral, offering no clear opinion of the book's writing or argument
quests.correctAnswer: Mixed: admiring the description but disappointed by the lack of analysis
quests.hint: Notice the turning point marked by "Yet".
quests.explanation: The reviewer praises the descriptions and the guides chapter but criticizes the missing argument.
quests.evidenceLine: the book keeps promising an argument it never delivers

quests.passage: [The Night Train to Inverness] There is no faster way to reach the Highlands than flying, but there is hardly a better one than the sleeper train. It leaves London at 9:15 p.m., and by the time passengers have eaten in the lounge car and negotiated their narrow bunks, the lights of the suburbs have gone. The ride is not silent; the carriages creak and the corridor doors bang. Yet I slept better than I do in most hotels, and woke to sheep-dotted hills in the pale morning. The train arrives at 10:30 a.m., about three hours later than a flight would, and costs a third less than the cheapest air fare. For anyone not in a hurry, it is the obvious choice.

The carriages creak and the corridor doors bang.

quests.passage: [The Woman Who Mapped the River] In 1921, Edith Marsh was hired as a clerk by the river authority, a job that involved filing survey reports. Within a year she noticed that two reports describing the same bend in the river disagreed by several hundred meters. Instead of ignoring the error, she spent her evenings comparing every report in the archive, and eventually produced a single corrected map. Her supervisors, who had not asked for it, were at first irritated by the extra work it created for the surveyors. But when floods hit the valley in 1927, it was Marsh's map that the engineers used to decide which villages to evacuate, and far fewer homes were lost than feared.

options: Her supervisors had asked her to do it.
The floods of 1927 forced the authority's hand.
She was promoted to the post of surveyor.
She noticed that two reports disagreed.
quests.correctAnswer: She noticed that two reports disagreed.
quests.hint: The cause appears in the second sentence.
quests.explanation: She spotted that two reports on the same bend differed by several hundred meters, and decided to check them all.
quests.evidenceLine: two reports describing the same bend in the river disagreed

Within a year she noticed that two reports describing the same bend in the river disagreed by several hundred meters. Instead of ignoring the error, she spent her evenings comparing every report in the archive, and eventually produced a single corrected map. Her supervisors, who had not asked for it, were at first irritated by the extra work it created for the surveyors. But when floods hit the valley in 1927, it was Marsh's map that the engineers used to decide which villages to evacuate, and far fewer homes were lost than feared.
quests.question: What does the passage suggest about the value of her initiative?
options: It was ignored by the authority for decades.
It cost the authority a great deal of money.
It proved useful in an emergency years later.
It caused confusion during the floods of 1927.
quests.correctAnswer: It proved useful in an emergency years later.
quests.hint: Compare the supervisors' first reaction with what happened in 1927.
quests.explanation: Though unwelcome at first, her map guided the evacuation decisions during the 1927 floods.
quests.evidenceLine: it was Marsh's map that the engineers used

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Radio Interview] Host: Rafael, your noodle stand has been on Cutler Street for twelve years. Has business changed? Rafael: The customers haven't. The costs have. Cooking oil is up forty percent since last year, and my rent went up in March. Host: Did you raise prices? Rafael: A little, twenty cents a bowl. Some regulars noticed, nobody complained. But I won't go higher. If a bowl costs more than a sandwich, people go for the sandwich. Host: So what's the solution? Rafael: I've cut the menu from nine dishes to five. Less waste, quicker service. Honestly, some days I think I'm working more for the landlord than for myself.
quests.question: What problem is Rafael describing?
options: A steady fall in the number of customers each week
Repeated complaints from regulars about his prices
Competition from a new noodle stand on the street
Higher costs that he cannot fully pass on to customers
quests.correctAnswer: Higher costs that he cannot fully pass on to customers
quests.hint: Notice the two short sentences that contrast customers with costs.
quests.explanation: His customers are unchanged but oil and rent cost more, and he cannot raise prices much without losing people.
quests.evidenceLine: The customers haven't. The costs have.
